\chapter{Out in the Paddy}
\label{ch:ml-out-in-the-paddy}
\hlchaptermodality{66}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name paddy, grass, an ear of grain, a plough and the harvest in Malayalam.}

Complete ML-C66-harvest and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nellŭ]{\ml{നെല്ല്} (nellŭ) — unhusked rice, rice still in the husk}

\label{lesson:ML-C66-paddy}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{maryāda} mean, and what did \emph{viśvāsaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{നെല്ല്}}
\textbf{\ml{നെല്ല്}} (\emph{nellŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}unhusked rice, rice still in the husk\textquotedblright{}.

Native Dravidian, matching Tamil \emph{nel}, and it completes a set you have been collecting a piece at a time. \ml{നെല്ല്} is the grain in the husk and in the field; \emph{ari} is the same grain husked; \emph{cōṟu} is it cooked.

Three words for one plant is what a language does when the plant is the year's whole work. The flooded field you already know by name, \emph{vayal}, is where the first of the three lives.

It sounds like \emph{ellŭ}, the bone-word, with an \emph{n} set in front. The two have nothing to do with one another, and the front of the word is again where the ear earns its keep.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five words from the paddy.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nellŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ellŭ}, then \emph{nellŭ}, and say which of the two you can eat
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{നെല്ല്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}unhusked rice, rice still in the husk\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pullŭ]{\ml{പുല്ല്} (pullŭ) — grass}

\label{lesson:ML-C66-grass}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nellŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{പുല്ല്}}
\textbf{\ml{പുല്ല്}} (\emph{pullŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}grass\textquotedblright{}.

Native Dravidian, matching Tamil \emph{pul}, and it ends the way \ml{നെല്ല്} ends — a doubled \emph{l} with the vowel shaved off, so the two words rhyme on the tail.

They are the field's two crops seen from opposite sides. One is planted and counted; the other turns up on its own and is cut for the animals.

Which makes this the \emph{paśu}'s word rather than the farmer's: grass is what the cow is walked out to.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pullŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{paśu}, then \emph{pullŭ}, and say which one eats the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{പുല്ല്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}grass\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[katirŭ]{\ml{കതിര്} (katirŭ) — an ear of ripe paddy}

\label{lesson:ML-C66-ear-of-grain}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{pullŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{കതിര്}}
\textbf{\ml{കതിര്}} (\emph{katirŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}an ear of ripe paddy\textquotedblright{}.

Native Dravidian, matching Tamil \emph{katir}, and the same word names a ray of light. The ear of grain and the sunbeam are one shape to this language: a narrow bright thing thrown out from a stem.

\emph{Veyil}, the sunshine-word, is the other half of that picture, and a Malayalam poet can put the two side by side and let the reader do the joining.

A field of \ml{കതിര്} is a field ready. Everything in this chapter after this point is what happens next.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{katirŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{veyil}, then \emph{katirŭ}, and say what the two have in common
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{കതിര്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}an ear of ripe paddy\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kalappa]{\ml{കലപ്പ} (kalappa) — a plough}

\label{lesson:ML-C66-plough}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{katirŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{കലപ്പ}}
\textbf{\ml{കലപ്പ}} (\emph{kalappa}) — \textquotedblleft{}a plough\textquotedblright{}.

Native Dravidian, and it names the tool behind a word you already carry. \emph{Karṣakan}, the farmer, was named for the furrow rather than for the crop; \ml{കലപ്പ} is what cuts the furrow.

Kerala's is a light wooden one, made for ground already under water, with a single iron-shod point and a beam for a pair of cattle.

Which puts the \emph{paśu} back to work: the animal of the first chapter in this run and the tool of the last one are yoked together.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kalappa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{karṣakan}, then \emph{kalappa}, and say which one holds the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{കലപ്പ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a plough\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[koyttŭ]{\ml{കൊയ്ത്ത്} (koyttŭ) — the harvest, the reaping}

\label{lesson:ML-C66-harvest}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kalappa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{കൊയ്ത്ത്}}
\textbf{\ml{കൊയ്ത്ത്}} (\emph{koyttŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}the harvest, the reaping\textquotedblright{}.

Native Dravidian, made from \emph{koyyuka}, to cut or to reap — the harvest named for the cutting rather than for the gathering that follows it.

Kerala's largest festival is the harvest festival, and the flower pattern laid at the doorway for it, \emph{pūkkaḷaṁ}, is the one the flower-lesson already named.

So the run closes where the year does: the grain, the grass, the ripe ear, the plough that opened the ground, and the cutting that ends it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the paddy year is whole: \emph{nellŭ}, \emph{pullŭ}, \emph{katirŭ}, \emph{kalappa}, \emph{koyttŭ}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{koyttŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{nellŭ}, \emph{pullŭ}, \emph{katirŭ}, \emph{kalappa}, \emph{koyttŭ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{കൊയ്ത്ത്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the harvest, the reaping\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
